steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on detecting whether a given text was part of a large language model's pretraining data, using only black-box access to the model. Motivate why this matters, explain why existing membership inference methods don't carry over to pretraining, and introduce our benchmark, our detection method and the case studies we ran.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: training data of LLMs is no longer disclosed, and why that is a problem
- Problem statement: pretraining data detection as membership inference, and its challenges
- Benchmark: WikiMIA
- Method: Min-k% Prob and main results
- Case studies and findings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - corpora growing; developers (GPT-4, LLaMA 2) reluctant to disclose composition/sources
  - lack of transparency -> problems for scientific evaluation, ethical deployment
  - private info exposed in pretraining: LLMs generated excerpts of copyrighted books, personal emails -> legal rights of creators, privacy
  - benchmark evaluation data may end up in pretraining corpus -> hard to assess models
- Problem statement
  - given text + black-box access to LLM, no knowledge of pretraining data: was the model pretrained on it?
  - we present benchmark WikiMIA + approach Min-k% Prob
  - instance of Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs); recent work: fine-tuning data detection as MIA
  - challenge 1: fine-tuning runs multiple epochs; pretraining = much larger data, each instance seen once -> less memorization
  - challenge 2: prior methods need reference models trained like target (shadow data from same distribution) -> not possible for LLMs (distribution unavailable, training too expensive)
- WikiMIA
  - dynamic benchmark, periodic + automatic evaluation of newly released pretrained LLMs
  - Wikipedia data timestamp + model release date: old event data = member (seen), recent event data (e.g. after 2023) = non-member (unseen)
  - properties: (1) Accurate - events after pretraining guaranteed absent; (2) General - any model pretrained on Wikipedia (OPT, LLaMA, GPT-Neo); (3) Dynamic - keep adding newer non-member data, pipeline fully automated
- Min-k% Prob
  - finetuning MIAs calibrate with shadow reference model on similar distribution -> impractical here (black-box data, compute cost)
  - reference-free; hypothesis: unseen example has a few low-probability outlier words, seen example less likely
  - computes average probabilities of outlier tokens; no knowledge of corpus, no extra training
  - beats strongest baseline by 7.4% AUC on WikiMIA
  - detection performance correlates positively with model size and text length
- Case studies
  - copyrighted book detection (§ 5), privacy auditing (§ 7), dataset contamination detection (§ 6); Min-k% Prob significantly better than baselines
  - evidence GPT-3 pretrained on copyrighted books from Books3
  - auditing machine unlearning: unlearned LLM trained to forget copyrighted books still outputs related copyrighted content
  - contamination: detection harder with larger training data, lower occurrence frequency of the example, lower learning rates

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
As language model (LM) training corpora have gotten larger, the developers of models (e.g, GPT-4 and LLaMA 2) don't want to disclose the full composition or sources of their data anymore. This lack of transparency is a critical challenge for scientific model evaluation and also for ethical deployment. Private information may be exposed during pretraining. Previous work showed that LLMs generated excerpts from copyrighted books and also personal emails, which potentially infringes upon the legal rights of the original content creators and violates their privacy. Also, other work showed that benchmark evaluation data may be included in the pretraining corpus by accident, which makes it difficult to assess how effective these models are.

In this paper we study the problem of pretraining data detection. Given a piece of text and black-box access to an LLM, with no knowledge of its pretraining data, can we determine if the model was pretrained on the text? We present a benchmark, WikiMIA, and an approach, Min-k% Prob, for this problem. The problem is an instance of Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs), which were initially proposed in earlier work. Recent work has studied fine-tuning data detection as an MIA problem. But adopting these methods to detect the pretraining data of contemporary large LLMs has two unique technical challenges. First, fine-tuning usually runs for multiple epochs, but pretraining uses a much larger dataset and exposes each instance only once, which significantly reduces the potential memorization that successful MIAs need. Second, previous methods often rely on one or more reference models that are trained in the same way as the target model (e.g., on shadow data sampled from the same underlying pretraining data distribution) to get precise detection. For large language models this is not possible, because the training distribution is usually not available and training would be too expensive.

Our first step towards addressing these challenges is to establish a reliable benchmark. We introduce WikiMIA, which is a dynamic benchmark designed to evaluate detection methods on any newly released pretrained LLMs, periodically and automatically. We use the Wikipedia data timestamp and the model release date to select the data: old Wikipedia event data is our member data (i.e., data seen during pretraining) and recent Wikipedia event data (e.g., after 2023) is our non-member data (unseen). So our datasets have three desirable properties. (1) Accurate: events that happen after LLM pretraining are guaranteed not to be in the pretraining data. (2) General: the benchmark can be applied to various models pretrained using Wikipedia (e.g., OPT, LLaMA, GPT-Neo). (3) Dynamic: we will keep updating it with newer non-member data, since the pipeline is fully automated.

- Min-k% Prob
  - finetuning MIAs calibrate with shadow reference model -> impractical here (black-box data, compute cost)
  - reference-free; hypothesis: unseen example has a few low-probability outlier words, seen example less likely
  - average probabilities of outlier tokens; no knowledge of corpus, no extra training
  - beats strongest baseline by 7.4% AUC on WikiMIA; performance correlates with model size and text length
- Case studies
  - copyrighted book detection (§ 5), privacy auditing (§ 7), dataset contamination detection (§ 6)
  - GPT-3 pretrained on copyrighted books from Books3
  - unlearned LLM still outputs related copyrighted content
  - contamination: harder with larger training data, lower occurrence frequency, lower learning rates

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
As language model (LM) training corpora have gotten larger, the developers of models (e.g, GPT-4 and LLaMA 2) don't want to disclose the full composition or sources of their data anymore. This lack of transparency is a critical challenge for scientific model evaluation and also for ethical deployment. Private information may be exposed during pretraining. Previous work showed that LLMs generated excerpts from copyrighted books and also personal emails, which potentially infringes upon the legal rights of the original content creators and violates their privacy. Also, other work showed that benchmark evaluation data may be included in the pretraining corpus by accident, which makes it difficult to assess how effective these models are.

In this paper we study the problem of pretraining data detection. Given a piece of text and black-box access to an LLM, with no knowledge of its pretraining data, can we determine if the model was pretrained on the text? We present a benchmark, WikiMIA, and an approach, Min-k% Prob, for this problem. The problem is an instance of Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs), which were initially proposed in earlier work. Recent work has studied fine-tuning data detection as an MIA problem. But adopting these methods to detect the pretraining data of contemporary large LLMs has two unique technical challenges. First, fine-tuning usually runs for multiple epochs, but pretraining uses a much larger dataset and exposes each instance only once, which significantly reduces the potential memorization that successful MIAs need. Second, previous methods often rely on one or more reference models that are trained in the same way as the target model (e.g., on shadow data sampled from the same underlying pretraining data distribution) to get precise detection. For large language models this is not possible, because the training distribution is usually not available and training would be too expensive.

Our first step towards addressing these challenges is to establish a reliable benchmark. We introduce WikiMIA, which is a dynamic benchmark designed to evaluate detection methods on any newly released pretrained LLMs, periodically and automatically. We use the Wikipedia data timestamp and the model release date to select the data: old Wikipedia event data is our member data (i.e., data seen during pretraining) and recent Wikipedia event data (e.g., after 2023) is our non-member data (unseen). So our datasets have three desirable properties. (1) Accurate: events that happen after LLM pretraining are guaranteed not to be in the pretraining data. Because events are temporal, the non-member data is really unseen and not mentioned in the pretraining data. (2) General: the benchmark is not confined to a specific model and can be applied to various models pretrained using Wikipedia (e.g., OPT, LLaMA, GPT-Neo), since Wikipedia is a commonly used pretraining data source. (3) Dynamic: we will keep updating our benchmark by gathering newer non-member data (i.e., more recent events) from Wikipedia, since our data construction pipeline is fully automated.

MIA methods for finetuning usually calibrate the target model probabilities of an example using a shadow reference model that is trained on a similar data distribution. These approaches are impractical for pretraining data detection, because of the black-box nature of pretraining data and its high computational cost. So we propose Min-k% Prob, a reference-free MIA method. The method is based on a simple hypothesis: an unseen example tends to contain a few outlier words with low probabilities, while a seen example is less likely to contain words with such low probabilities. Min-k% Prob computes the average probabilities of the outlier tokens. It can be applied without any knowledge about the pretraining corpus or any additional training, which is different from existing MIA methods that rely on shadow reference models. In our experiments Min-k% Prob outperforms the existing strongest baseline by 7.4% in AUC score on WikiMIA. Further analysis suggests that the detection performance correlates positively with the model size and with the length of the text being detected.

To verify that our method is applicable in real-world settings, we do three case studies: copyrighted book detection (§ 5), privacy auditing of LLMs (§ 7) and dataset contamination detection (§ 6). Min-k% Prob significantly outperforms baseline methods in these scenarios. From the copyrighted book detection experiments, we see strong evidence that GPT-3 is pretrained on copyrighted books from the Books3 dataset. In the privacy auditing experiments on machine unlearning, we use Min-k% Prob to audit an unlearned LLM that is trained to forget copyrighted books using machine unlearning techniques, and we find the model could still output related copyrighted content. Also, our controlled study on dataset contamination detection sheds light on how pretraining design choices affect detection difficulty. Detection gets harder when training data sizes increase, and when the occurrence frequency of the detecting example and the learning rates decrease.

steps.text:
As the scale of language model (LM) training corpora has grown, model developers (e.g, GPT-4 [1] and LLaMA 2 [2]) have become reluctant to disclose the full composition or sources of their data. This lack of transparency poses critical challenges to scientific model evaluation and to ethical deployment. Critical private information may be exposed during pretraining; previous work showed that LLMs generated excerpts from copyrighted books [3] and personal emails [4], potentially infringing upon the legal rights of the original content creators and violating their privacy. In addition, [5,6,7] showed that the pretraining corpus may inadvertently include benchmark evaluation data, making it difficult to assess the effectiveness of these models.

In this paper, we study the pretraining data detection problem: given a piece of text and black-box access to an LLM with no knowledge of its pretraining data, can we determine if the model was pretrained on the text? We present a benchmark, WikiMIA, and an approach, Min-k% Prob, for pretraining data detection. This problem is an instance of Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs), which was initially proposed by [8]. Recent work has studied fine-tuning data detection [9,10,11] as an MIA problem. However, adopting these methods to detect the pretraining data of contemporary large LLMs presents two unique technical challenges. First, unlike fine-tuning, which usually runs for multiple epochs, pretraining uses a much larger dataset but exposes each instance only once, significantly reducing the potential memorization needed for successful MIAs [12,13]. Second, previous methods often rely on one or more reference models [14,15] trained in the same manner as the target model (e.g., on shadow data sampled from the same underlying pretraining data distribution) to achieve precise detection. This is not possible for large language models, as the training distribution is usually not available and training would be too expensive.

Our first step towards addressing these challenges is to establish a reliable benchmark. We introduce WikiMIA, a dynamic benchmark designed to periodically and automatically evaluate detection methods on any newly released pretrained LLMs. Using the Wikipedia data timestamp and the model release date, we select old Wikipedia event data as our member data (i.e, seen data during pretraining) and recent Wikipedia event data (e.g., after 2023) as our non-member data (unseen). (2) General: our benchmark is not confined to any specific model and can be applied to various models pretrained using Wikipedia (e.g., OPT, LLaMA, GPT-Neo), since Wikipedia is a commonly used pretraining data source. (3) Dynamic: since our data construction pipeline is fully automated, we will continually update our benchmark by gathering newer non-member data (i.e., more recent events) from Wikipedia.

We therefore propose a reference-free MIA method, Min-k% Prob. Our method is based on a simple hypothesis: an unseen example tends to contain a few outlier words with low probabilities, whereas a seen example is less likely to contain words with such low probabilities. Min-k% Prob computes the average probabilities of outlier tokens. It can be applied without any knowledge about the pretraining corpus or any additional training, departing from existing MIA methods, which rely on shadow reference models [16,17]. From our copyrighted book detection experiments, we see strong evidence that GPT-3 is pretrained on copyrighted books from the Books3 dataset [18,19]. In our experiments on privacy auditing of machine unlearning, we use Min-k% Prob to audit an unlearned LLM that is trained to forget copyrighted books using machine unlearning techniques [20], and find that such a model could still output related copyrighted content. Furthermore, our controlled study on dataset contamination detection sheds light on the impact of pretraining design choices on detection difficulty: detection becomes harder when training data sizes increase, and when the occurrence frequency of the detecting example and the learning rate decrease.
